title: That Which We Have Seen and Heard
subtitle: 1 John 1:1–4
description: An eyewitness opening with no name signed: a life heard, seen, and touched, proclaimed so the hearers may share the fellowship and the joy be complete.
paragraphs: The letter begins without a greeting, without a name, and without an address, and its first sentence reaches back past every event it will touch: “That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our own eyes, which we have gazed upon and touched with our own hands.” The verbs climb the senses one at a time. Heard first, then seen with our own eyes, then gazed upon, the longer look, and at the top of the climb, touched with our own hands. Whatever this letter is about, the writer plants its authority in a body that could be handled. The sentence finishes on the far side of its own break, naming the thing handled: “this is the Word of life.” Word and life in one phrase, something spoken and something alive, and the man writing claims his hands were on it.

What was handled was also given. “And this is the life that was revealed; we have seen it and testified to it, and we proclaim to you the eternal life that was with the Father and was revealed to us.” Revealed is the word doing the work: the life was with the Father, hidden in the way a thing is hidden before it is shown, and then it was shown, and the showing is what the witnesses testify to. Proclaim is their verb, not invent and not improve. The eternal life is not their discovery to keep or their idea to spread. It was with the Father, it was revealed to them, and now it is proclaimed to the readers, in that order, with the witnesses standing in the middle as witnesses and nothing more.

The proclamation has a destination, and the destination is not information. “We proclaim to you what we have seen and heard, so that you also may have fellowship with us. And this fellowship of ours is with the Father and with His Son, Jesus Christ.” Fellowship is the goal of the telling: a shared life the readers are invited inside, not a set of facts they are asked to admire from outside. And the fellowship already has an address. It is with the Father and with his Son, Jesus Christ, named here in the letter's third verse, the first time the writer names him. The circle runs in one motion: the life revealed to the witnesses, proclaimed to the hearers, and the hearers brought into the same fellowship the witnesses have with the Father and the Son.

The writer never names himself in this letter, and the telling follows him in that. Tradition has long ascribed the letter to John the apostle, and that ascription is named here once, as tradition. What the letter itself gives is a voice: an eyewitness “we” that heard and saw and touched, and, as the letter goes on, a father in the faith who calls his readers his little children. His standing in these pages rests on the testimony he states and on nothing the telling adds to it. The book stands in the undated group of this series, with no date given and none invented, and the Gospel that carries the story of Jesus in full stands in its own place in the series, pointed to and not retold here.

One more purpose is stated before the opening ends, and it is warmer than argument. “We write these things so that our joy may be complete.” Not so that the readers may be corrected, though correction is coming in this letter, and not so that a case may be won, though a case will be made. Joy, and joy completed, is the writer's own account of why the letter exists, his joy and theirs bound in the same word our. Four verses carry the whole foundation: a life from the beginning, handled by witnesses, revealed and proclaimed, fellowship opened, and joy as the motive. From that foundation the letter turns, in its next breath, to the message the witnesses heard from him, and the message is a single claim about God: he is light, and in him there is no darkness at all.

title: God Is Light
subtitle: 1 John 1:5–10
description: God is light with no darkness at all; the walk tested, sin confessed, and forgiveness promised by a faithful and just God.
paragraphs: The witnesses now deliver what they received. “And this is the message we have heard from Him and announce to you: God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all.” Heard from him, announced to you: the letter keeps its chain of custody in plain sight. And the message itself is one claim with a total denial built into it. God is light, not mostly light, not light with shaded corners, and in him there is no darkness at all. The at all is the writer's own emphasis, and everything in the next six verses is this one claim walked out into the lives of the people who say they believe it.

The first test is the walk. “If we say we have fellowship with Him yet walk in the darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth.” The claim and the walk are set side by side, and where they contradict, the walk is believed. But the verse that follows is not a threat; it is a promise with the same shape. “But if we walk in the light as He is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin.” Walking in the light does not mean standing where no sin can reach. It lands the walker in two gifts at once: fellowship with one another, restored sideways, and cleansing from all sin, flowing from the blood of Jesus. The light exposes and cleanses in the same step.

Then the letter turns its claim on the reader's own mouth. “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” The first liar in this letter's gallery of liars is not the false teacher; it is the man describing himself. Self-deception is the diagnosis, and it is stated as a condition any of the hearers can be in, we-language, the writer including his own circle in the warning's reach. A person walking in the light of a God with no darkness in him will see his own sin more clearly, not less, and the claim to have none is itself the evidence that the truth is not in him.

Against that deception stands one practice, stated with a double promise. “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” Confession is the whole assignment: name the sins, and the rest of the verse belongs to God. He is faithful, so the forgiveness is sure; he is just, so the forgiveness is right, not a winking exception; and the outcome runs past pardon to cleansing, from all unrighteousness, the same total register as the cleansing from all sin. The letter's most quoted verse is also its most complete: human honesty on one side, divine faithfulness on the other, and nothing left over between them.

The passage ends at its sharpest point, and the sharpness is deliberate. “If we say we have not sinned, we make Him out to be a liar, and His word is not in us.” The claim that began as self-deception ends as an accusation against God: since he has said all have sinned, the man who denies his own sin is calling the witness of verse one a liar. That is where the first chapter stops, with no softening sentence after it. But the letter does not leave the sinner there. Its next words take up the very person these verses describe, the one who does sin, and name the help standing ready for him before the Father.

title: Christ Our Advocate
subtitle: 1 John 2:1–6
description: A father aims that his children not sin, the advocate stands ready if they do, and knowledge of God is tested by keeping his commandments.
paragraphs: The second chapter opens with the letter's most tender address and its sternest aim held in one sentence. “My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you will not sin.” My little children: the eyewitness of the opening verses writes as a father, and the purpose of everything just said about light and confession is prevention, that his children will not sin. The tenderness is not indulgence. A father who wants his children kept from a cliff edge writes exactly this way, warmly and without a wasted word, and then immediately prepares for the case he is trying to prevent.

The preparation is the verse's second half, and it is carried as the text breaks it: “But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate before the Father” and then the name, set off as the letter sets it off, “Jesus Christ, the Righteous One.” An advocate is a spokesman for the defense, someone who stands beside the accused and speaks in the room where judgment sits. The sinning believer has one, present tense, we have, and his qualification is the opposite of his client's: he is the Righteous One, the one man in the room with no sin of his own to answer for. The father writes so his children will not sin; he also writes so that when they do, they will know the first fact about their case.

The advocate's standing rests on what he did, and the next verse gives it the widest scope in the letter. “He Himself is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not only for ours but also for the sins of the whole world.” He himself: the advocate is the sacrifice, the same person on both sides of the case. And the reach of the sacrifice runs past the fellowship's own circle to the whole world, a breadth the telling carries at full strength the way he states it. The little children reading this letter are not holding a private remedy. The sacrifice that covers them is as wide as the world that will shortly be warned against, and the letter sees no strain in holding both.

From the advocate the letter turns to a question its readers would naturally ask: how can we be sure we know him? “By this we can be sure that we have come to know Him: if we keep His commandments.” Knowledge of God is tested the way the walk was tested, by obedience, and the negative form is as blunt as anything in the first chapter. A man says, “I know Him,” and the saying stands alone in its own quotation, and then the verdict follows outside it: “but does not keep His commandments, he is a liar, and the truth is not in him.” The liar word returns, aimed now at the man whose claim of knowledge floats free of his life. Against him stands the opposite pattern: “But if anyone keeps His word, the love of God has been truly perfected in him.” Keeping the word is where God's love reaches its goal in a person.

The paragraph ends with the measure that governs them all: “Whoever claims to abide in Him must walk as Jesus walked.” Abiding is the letter's great word for the settled life in God, and its test is a walk measured against a walk: as Jesus walked. Not as Jesus is admired, or as Jesus is confessed, but as he walked, step-shaped, in the open. That sentence is the hinge of the whole section. What follows takes up the commandment behind the keeping, and finds it is both the oldest thing the readers own and, in the light now shining, something new.

title: An Old Commandment, Ever New
subtitle: 1 John 2:7–14
description: The commandment old from the beginning and new in the shining light, love and hate as addresses, and a poem to children, fathers, and young men.
paragraphs: The writer now corrects an impression before it forms. “Beloved, I am not writing to you a new commandment, but an old one, which you have had from the beginning.” The commandment behind the keeping of the last verses is not an innovation and not his invention; the readers have had it from the beginning of their own hearing. Then, in the very next breath, he reverses the direction without canceling it: “Then again, I am also writing to you a new commandment, which is true in Him and also in you. For the darkness is fading and the true light is already shining.” Old as their first hearing, new as the situation it now operates in: the darkness is fading, present tense, and the true light is already shining, and a commandment about loving the brother means something more in a world where the light has actually come than it could mean as a rumor of light.

The test that follows is the light test aimed at a relationship. “If anyone claims to be in the light but hates his brother, he is still in the darkness.” Still is the cutting word: whatever enlightenment the man claims, the hatred locates him, and he has not moved. The opposite is stated just as plainly: “Whoever loves his brother remains in the light, and there is no cause of stumbling in him.” Love keeps a man in the light and clears his path of the thing he would trip on. And the hater's condition is drawn to its end: “But whoever hates his brother is in the darkness and walks in the darkness. He does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.” The darkness outside becomes darkness inside, until the man loses even his direction. Love and hate are not feelings in this letter's accounting. They are addresses, and a man lives at one of them.

Then the letter pauses its warnings and does something unexpected: it sings to its readers in a patterned address, children, fathers, young men, and then again. “I am writing to you, little children, because your sins have been forgiven through His name.” “I am writing to you, fathers, because you know Him who is from the beginning.” “I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one.” The rounds repeat with small additions, the children knowing the Father, the fathers knowing him who is from the beginning a second time, and the young men filled out: “because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome the evil one.” Whether the three groups are ages of the body or stages of the life, the letter does not say, and the telling leaves them as he arranges them, three names for the whole family spoken to at once.

What the poem says about these readers matters for everything around it. They are forgiven. They know the Father. The fathers among them know the one from the beginning, the young men are strong, God's word abides in them, and the evil one has already been overcome by them. The warnings of this letter are not written to people on the edge of the faith looking in. They are written to the established, the forgiven, the strong, and that is exactly why the next warning can land so hard: a settled people can still set its love on the wrong world, and the letter turns next to the love that must be refused.

title: Do Not Love the World
subtitle: 1 John 2:15–17
description: The world and its three desires named and refused, a system already passing away set against the one who does the will of God and remains forever.
paragraphs: The warning arrives as a command with no cushion. “Do not love the world or anything in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.” World here is not the earth God made and not the whole world whose sins the advocate's sacrifice covers; it is the world's system of wanting, the order of things organized against the Father, and the verse treats two loves as tenants who cannot share one house. Love of the world moves in, and the love of the Father is not in him. The letter does not say the two loves compete or crowd each other. It says one excludes the other, flatly, and leaves the reader to examine which love is resident.

Then the contents of the world are inventoried, and the inventory is three lines long. The verse itself breaks around its own list, so the telling carries it the way it is written: “For all that is in the world” and then the list itself, “the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes, and the pride of life,” and then the verdict on the whole inventory, “is not from the Father but from the world.” Wanting that starts in the flesh, wanting that starts in the eyes, and the pride that puffs a life up into its own display: appetite, acquisition, and advertisement, as old as a garden and as current as this morning. None of it, he says, has the Father for its source. It is from the world, and the world is the only place it can be from.

The command's reason is not that the world is strong. The reason is that the world is ending. “The world is passing away, along with its desires; but whoever does the will of God remains forever.” Passing away is present tense: the thing being loved is already in the act of leaving, taking its desires with it, and love invested in it is invested in a departure. Against that stands one figure who remains, not the one who felt the right things about God but the one who does the will of God, and the remaining is forever. The whole letter's architecture of light and darkness, passing and remaining, stands in this verse at its smallest scale: three verses, three contents, two destinies.

It is a short passage, and the letter does not linger on it. Love has been tested by the walk, by the commandments, by the brother, and now by the world itself, and each test has used the same method, a claim checked against a reality. The next test is harder, because it concerns people who once stood inside the fellowship and now stand outside it preaching, and the writer names the hour his readers are living in with two of the most charged words in the letter: the last hour.

title: The Last Hour
subtitle: 1 John 2:18–27
description: The last hour named, the many antichrists identified by their denial, and the ones who went out from us answered by the anointing that remains.
paragraphs: The hour is named first. “Children, it is the last hour; and just as you have heard that the antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have appeared. This is how we know it is the last hour.” The readers had been told to expect an antichrist, singular, a figure of the end. What has arrived instead is plural: many antichrists, already here, and their arrival is itself the evidence for the hour. The telling carries his claim at the strength he makes it, with no timetable built on it and no later age's figures matched to it. The last hour, in this letter, is not a date to calculate. It is the name of the time his readers are already standing in, and the proof is standing in front of them.

The proof has a history, and he gives it in the letter's most sorrowful verse. “They went out from us, but they did not belong to us. For if they had belonged to us, they would have remained with us. But their departure made it clear that none of them belonged to us.” The antichrists did not invade from outside; they departed from inside, people who had stood in the fellowship and walked out of it. His reading of the departure is theological, not just sad: leaving revealed what membership had concealed. They went out because they were not of us, and the going made it clear. The telling carries his account at his strength, naming no group beyond his words and filling in no names, dates, or doctrines he does not name.

Against the departed stands what the remaining ones hold. “You, however, have an anointing from the Holy One, and all of you know the truth.” The anointing, given by the Holy One and remaining in them, is the letter's answer to deception: not a cleverer argument but a gift that stays. And lest the warnings be misread as doubt about his readers, he states his reason for writing with unusual care: “I have not written to you because you lack knowledge of the truth, but because you have it, and because no lie comes from the truth.” They know. The letter arms people who already hold the truth; it does not treat them as empty.

The lie itself is then defined at its root. “Who is the liar, if it is not the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist, who denies the Father and the Son.” After the liars of self-deception and empty claims, here is the liar in full: the denial that Jesus is the Christ, and with it, necessarily, the denial of the Father who sent him. The pairing is inseparable: “Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father, but whoever confesses the Son has the Father as well.” There is no route to the Father running around the Son in this letter, in either direction, and confession and denial are the two doors.

The section closes by handing the readers their one assignment, and it is the letter's master word again: remain. “As for you, let what you have heard from the beginning remain in you.” “And this is the promise that He Himself made to us: eternal life.” “I have written these things to you about those who are trying to deceive you.” And the anointing itself teaches: “the anointing you received from Him remains in you, and you do not need anyone to teach you.” Remain in what was heard from the beginning, remain in him as taught, and the deception fails on its own. The next movement of the letter picks up the same word and turns it toward a Person's appearing, and toward the family name the readers carry: children of God.

title: Children of God
subtitle: 1 John 2:28–3:10
description: Called children of God, and that is what we are; the hope that purifies, and the letter's strongest sentences on sin standing at full strength.
paragraphs: The remaining has a reason, and the reason is an appearing. “And now, little children, remain in Christ, so that when He appears, we may be confident and unashamed before Him at His coming.” Confidence at his coming is the goal of the abiding, and shame is its opposite, and the hinge between them is staying where they already are. One more premise is laid down before the chapter turns: if he is righteous, then “everyone who practices righteousness has been born of Him.” Birth, not effort, is the ground of the practice, and with birth named, the letter lifts its eyes to the fact itself and marvels at it.

“Behold what manner of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God. And that is what we are!” Behold is an invitation to stare. The love is measured by the name it gives: children of God, not servants improved or subjects pardoned but children, and the exclamation that follows guards against treating the name as a courtesy title: that is what we are. The world's failure to recognize them is explained in one line and dismissed in the same line: “The reason the world does not know us is that it did not know Him.” Non-recognition runs in the family. It happened to him first.

The present name carries a future that is still veiled, and the letter is precise about both halves. “Beloved, we are now children of God, and what we will be has not yet been revealed. We know that when Christ appears, we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is.” Now is solid, the future is unfinished, and what is known about the future is likeness: seeing him as he is produces being like him. The hope is not decorative. “And everyone who has this hope in Him purifies himself, just as Christ is pure.” Hope aimed at that appearing does present-tense work in the person holding it, and with that, the letter turns from the children's hope to the sharpest statements it makes anywhere about sin.

The turn is a definition first: “Everyone who practices sin practices lawlessness as well. Indeed, sin is lawlessness.” Then the purpose of the first appearing is set against the practice: “But you know that Christ appeared to take away sins, and in Him there is no sin.” And then the sentences the telling carries at full strength, exactly as written, softened for no one and aimed at no one: “No one who remains in Him keeps on sinning. No one who continues to sin has seen Him or known Him.” The writer warns against deception precisely here, “let no one deceive you,” and names the devil's long career as the opposing pattern: “because the devil has been sinning from the very start. This is why the Son of God was revealed, to destroy the works of the devil.”

The strongest sentence is the last one, and it rests the whole matter on the birth already celebrated: “Anyone born of God refuses to practice sin, because God’s seed abides in him; he cannot go on sinning, because he has been born of God.” The letter does not reconcile this with its own first chapter, where the man who says he has no sin deceives himself and confession is the standing remedy; it sets both at full strength in their places and leaves them standing together, the confession of chapter one and the birth of chapter three, and the telling does the same. The section's own summary is a distinction, stated as a fact of the family: “By this the children of God are distinguished from the children of the devil: Anyone who does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is anyone who does not love his brother.” Righteousness and brother-love arrive joined, and the letter takes the second of the pair up next, back to the message heard from the beginning.

title: Love One Another
subtitle: 1 John 3:11–18
description: Love one another, the message from the beginning; Cain as the category of hatred, and love defined by a life laid down and tested at the open hand.
paragraphs: The letter returns to its oldest sentence. “This is the message you have heard from the beginning: We should love one another.” From the beginning is the letter's refrain for the commandment: heard at the start, carried through every test since, and now stated as the message itself, with nothing added. Love of the brother is not one topic among the letter's topics. By this point it has been the light test, the knowledge test, and the birth test, and here it simply stands as the message, the way it stood at their first hearing.

Its negative example is the Bible's first murderer, carried in the letter's own compression: “Do not be like Cain, who belonged to the evil one and murdered his brother. And why did Cain slay him? Because his own deeds were evil, while those of his brother were righteous.” No garden scene is retold here and no offering is described; Cain's whole story lives in the Genesis book of this series, pointed to and not re-expanded. What the letter extracts is the motive, and the motive is the deeds: evil deeds hating righteous ones. That is the template the writer sets behind all brother-hatred, and it explains the sentence that follows without surprise: “So do not be surprised, brothers, if the world hates you.” The world hated the righteous brother first.

Then the letter states its most astonishing piece of self-knowledge. “We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love our brothers.” Of all the evidences this letter offers, and it offers many, this is the one attached to the largest claim: the passage from death to life, already accomplished, known by the love of the brothers. Its negative is equally plain: “The one who does not love remains in death.” And the hatred that keeps a man there is weighed in the letter's hardest words on the subject: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that eternal life does not reside in a murderer.” Cain is not an ancient exception. He is the category, and hatred is membership in it.

Against the category stands the definition of love itself, given the same way the letter defined it before, by an event. “By this we know what love is: Jesus laid down His life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers.” We know what love is, not by a feeling measured but by a life laid down, and the definition immediately becomes a debt: we ought, in the same direction, with our own lives. Love in this letter is never a sentiment looking for expression. It is a pattern set by a death and owed by the living.

The passage ends by bringing the debt down to the scale of a wallet, and the smallness is the point. “If anyone with earthly possessions sees his brother in need, but withholds his compassion from him, how can the love of God abide in him?” A brother in need, possessions in hand, compassion withheld: the question answers itself, and it is aimed at people who would readily affirm the laying-down of lives. Most love's failures do not happen at the scale of martyrdom. They happen at the scale of the closed hand. So the closing charge matches the scale of the test: “Little children, let us love not in word and speech, but in action and truth.” The next verses take up what such love does for the heart that practices it, and the assurance it builds before God.

title: Hearts at Rest Before Him
subtitle: 1 John 3:19–24
description: Hearts assured in God's presence, God greater than our hearts, and the one commandment fusing belief in the Son's name with love for one another.
paragraphs: Love in action does something for the lover, and this short passage names it: assurance. “And by this we will know that we belong to the truth, and will assure our hearts in His presence:” The by this reaches back to the love just described, the kind that opens its hand. Belonging to the truth is not only argued in this letter; it is felt, in a heart assured in God's presence rather than shrinking from it. What follows is the most pastorally careful sentence in the letter, because it deals with the heart that will not be assured.

“Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts, and He knows all things.” The verdict of a condemning heart is real, and the writer does not call it imaginary. He appeals it to a higher court: God is greater than our hearts, and his knowledge is total where the heart's is partial. The sentence cuts in both directions at once, and the telling leaves both edges on it. The heart that condemns too harshly is overruled by a God who knows all things; the heart that would acquit too easily faces the same knowledge. What the verse gives the troubled reader is not a smaller God but a greater one, greater than the courtroom inside his own chest.

The other case is stated just as calmly. “Beloved, if our hearts do not condemn us, we have confidence before God,” and the confidence has a practical address: “and we will receive from Him whatever we ask, because we keep His commandments and do what is pleasing in His sight.” Answered prayer in this letter is not a technique. It sits inside the same structure as everything else, a life of kept commandments and pleased-God living, confidence before God flowing from a heart at rest in him. The ask and the obedience are not traded for each other; they grow in the same soil.

Then the commandments that have filled the letter are suddenly gathered into one, and the one has two halves. “And this is His commandment: that we should believe in the name of His Son, Jesus Christ, and we should love one another just as He commanded us.” Singular commandment, believe and love, faith in the name of the Son and love of the brothers bound as a single instruction. Everything the letter has separated into tests, it here fuses: believing and loving are not two religions but one commandment with a name in it.

The passage closes on the ground of all the knowing in it. “Whoever keeps His commandments remains in God, and God in him. And by this we know that He remains in us: by the Spirit He has given us.” The Spirit given is the evidence of the mutual remaining, God's presence attested from inside the life itself. That naming of the Spirit is the letter's bridge: having said God remains in us by the Spirit he gave, the next chapter opens by warning that not every spirit is his, and the spirits must be tested.

title: Test the Spirits
subtitle: 1 John 4:1–6
description: Test the spirits by one confession, Jesus Christ come in the flesh; greater is he who is in you than he who is in the world.
paragraphs: Having named the Spirit God gave, the letter immediately warns against trusting every voice that claims him. “Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God. For many false prophets have gone out into the world.” Beloved opens the warning the way a father opens it, warmly and firmly: belief is not to be indiscriminate. The spirits behind the teachers are to be tested, examined like metal, because the traffic is real: many false prophets have gone out, the same going-out the secession described, now named as a mission into the world.

The test itself is one confession. “By this you will know the Spirit of God: Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God,” and its refusal is the opposite mark: “and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you have heard is coming and which is already in the world at this time.” The flesh is the battleground: Jesus Christ come in the flesh, real arrival in real humanity, the same handled and touched reality the letter opened with. Denial of it is not a lesser opinion in this accounting. It is the spirit of the antichrist, future and present at once, coming and already here, carried at the strength he states it with no figure in any age matched to it.

Then, before the readers can feel outnumbered, the verdict on their own standing: “You, little children, are from God and have overcome them, because greater is He who is in you than he who is in the world.” Overcome is past tense. The contest between the children and the prophets is described as already decided, and the reason is a comparison of residents: he who is in you against he who is in the world, and the greater is named without argument. The little children carry the stronger indwelling, and the letter tells them so in the middle of the warning, not after it.

The world's teachers have their own audience, and its existence proves nothing. “They are of the world. That is why they speak from the world’s perspective, and the world listens to them.” Speech from the world finds hearing in the world; popularity is a matching of sources, not a test of truth. The letter gives its readers a colder and better instrument than applause, and it turns, in the last verse, on the witnesses themselves: “We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. That is how we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of deception.” The apostolic we of the opening returns as a test: hearing or refusing the testimony sorts the hearers.

Two spirits are on the table now, truth and deception, and the tests are christological and communal at once: what is confessed about Jesus in the flesh, and whether the testimony is heard. From the spirits the letter swings, without transition, to its greatest subject, announced as a call to the beloved for the fourth time in the letter: let us love one another, because God himself is love.

title: God Is Love
subtitle: 1 John 4:7–12
description: God is love, defined by the sending of his Son, and the unseen God answered by love practiced among the brothers.
paragraphs: The call comes with its reason attached, and the reason is God's nature. “Beloved, let us love one another, because love comes from God. Everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God.” Love is not manufactured in the lover; it comes from God the way light comes from the sun, and loving is therefore evidence of birth and knowledge, the letter's two great family facts. The negative stands in the next verse without decoration: “Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love.” This is the letter's second great claim about God, matching the first chapter's: God is light, and God is love. Neither is a metaphor he qualifies. Love is not something God does on occasion; it is what he is, and the person with no love has no knowledge of such a God, whatever else he knows.

The claim is immediately given its evidence, and the evidence is an event. “This is how God’s love was revealed among us: God sent His one and only Son into the world, so that we might live through Him.” Love was revealed the way the life was revealed in the letter's opening, by a sending. The Son is one and only, the sending is into the world, and the purpose is life for the receivers, life through him. God is love could have remained a saying; the writer anchors it to a mission with a name and a destination, so that the nature of God is read off an act of God.

Then he defines love itself, and the definition runs backwards from the natural direction. “And love consists in this: not that we loved God, but that He loved us and sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins.” Love consists in this: not our love reaching up but his love coming down, and its instrument is the same atoning sacrifice the advocate passage named, the Son sent to be it. Every later human love in this letter is a response, a copy, an owing, never the original. The definition is built to kill pride in the lover: the first move was God's, made while the receivers were sinners in need of a sacrifice.

The owing follows in one sentence, and its logic is the letter's whole ethic in miniature. “Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.” If God so loved: so, in that manner, at that cost, in that direction. The ought is not pressure to manufacture a feeling; it is the shape of a life that has received that love, the way a lit lamp ought to shine. The measure of the love owed to the brother is the love received from God, and the letter will not lower either side of the comparison.

The section ends on a paradox and resolves it with the brothers. “No one has ever seen God; but if we love one another, God remains in us, and His love is perfected in us.” No one has ever seen God: the unseen God of the fourth chapter's end is already here. The answer is not a vision granted to a few. It is love practiced among the many, and through that practice God remains in his people and his love reaches its goal, perfected, in them. The invisible God becomes present in the visible love. What follows takes up the confidence this produces, and the fear it drives out.

title: Perfect Love Drives Out Fear
subtitle: 1 John 4:13–21
description: Perfect love drives out fear, the liar charged one last time, and the commandment joining love of God with love of his brother.
paragraphs: The knowing returns first, grounded where the letter keeps grounding it. “By this we know that we remain in Him, and He in us: He has given us of His Spirit.” And the testimony stands beside the gift: “And we have seen and testify that the Father has sent His Son to be the Savior of the world.” Seen and testify, the eyewitness verbs of the first chapter, now carrying the largest title the letter gives Jesus: Savior of the world. The response asked of the hearer is confession, and its promise is mutual abiding: “If anyone confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God.”

Then the great claim is repeated and personalized. The witnesses “have come to know and believe the love that God has for us,” and then, for the second time, “God is love; whoever abides in love abides in God, and God in him.” The repetition is the letter's method at its clearest: the same truth circled again, this time to land on a day. “In this way, love has been perfected among us, so that we may have confidence on the day of judgment; for in this world we are just like Him.” Love perfected among the brothers produces confidence aimed at the day of judgment itself, stated as he states it with no timetable attached, and its ground is a likeness: in this world, now, we are just like him, and so the day holds no terror of meeting a stranger.

The fear sentence follows, and it is carried in the letter's own words: “There is no fear in love, but perfect love drives out fear, because fear involves punishment. The one who fears has not been perfected in love.” Drives out is the verb, eviction language: perfected love does not manage fear or balance it; it expels it, because fear's fuel is punishment, the expectation of a settling of accounts, and love completed leaves nothing for that expectation to feed on. The fearful man is not scolded. He is described: not yet perfected in love, which makes fear a stage to grow out of rather than a verdict to despair under. And the root of the whole growth is dated before any of it: “We love because He first loved us.” First is the load-bearing word.

The liar returns one final time, and the spoken claim stands alone in its own quotation the way this letter handles such claims: a man says, “I love God,” and then the verdict outside the quotation: “but hates his brother, he is a liar.” The reasoning is a plain matter of sight: “For anyone who does not love his brother, whom he has seen, cannot love God, whom he has not seen.” Love that fails at the visible brother and claims success at the invisible God is graded a lie, not a weakness, and the letter gives the man no third category.

The section, and with it the letter's whole teaching on love, closes with a commandment, not a summary. “And we have this commandment from Him: Whoever loves God must love his brother as well.” From him is the authority, must is the force, and the two loves the letter has spent four chapters joining are joined in law at the end of them. One movement remains: the letter turns to faith that overcomes the world, and to the witnesses who testify to the Son.

title: The Three That Testify
subtitle: 1 John 5:1–12
description: Faith the victory that overcomes the world, and the three witnesses in agreement: the Spirit, the water, and the blood.
paragraphs: The last chapter opens with the family circle drawn complete. “Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and everyone who loves the Father also loves those born of Him.” Belief, birth, and family love arrive in one sentence, and the test of the family love is the same as ever: “By this we know that we love the children of God: when we love God and keep His commandments.” Then a sentence that reframes the whole letter's demands: “For this is the love of God, that we keep His commandments. And His commandments are not burdensome,” The commandments that test everything are not a weight strapped to the believer. The letter has called them old and new, singular and plural; now it calls them light to carry, for a reason the next verse supplies.

The reason is victory. “because everyone born of God overcomes the world. And this is the victory that has overcome the world: our faith.” The world that must not be loved is also a world that can be overcome, and the overcoming instrument is not strength or discipline but faith. The question that follows names its holder: “Who then overcomes the world? Only he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God.” Belief in Jesus as the Son of God, the confession that has sorted every spirit and every hearer in the letter, is also the victory. The world is overcome not by escaping it but by believing rightly about the one sent into it.

Then the letter turns to testimony, and the first witness statement concerns how the Son came. The verse breaks around its own correction, so the telling carries it as written: “This is the One who came by water and blood, Jesus Christ” and then the correction itself, “not by water alone, but by water and blood.” Both, he insists, water and blood together, and the telling adds no theory of what the water and the blood map onto beyond his insistence that the coming was by both. The third witness is a person: “And it is the Spirit who testifies to this, because the Spirit is the truth.”

The testimony is then counted. “For there are three that testify:” and the three are named across the verse break, “the Spirit, the water, and the blood” and the agreement is stated as the verse itself breaks to state it, “and these three are in agreement.” The telling adds no other witnesses and imports no longer list; three are named, and their agreement is the fact. Agreement is what testimony needs to stand, and God's testimony outranks the human kind on the letter's own scale: “Even if we accept human testimony, the testimony of God is greater.” And this testimony has an address and a content. It is the testimony God has given about his Son, and the believer carries it inside: whoever believes has this testimony within him, while whoever refuses it has made God out to be a liar, the letter's liar charge arriving at its final and most serious form, aimed not at a false claim about oneself or one's brother but at disbelief of God's own witness.

The content of the testimony is one sentence, and it gathers the letter's whole promise: “And this is that testimony: God has given us eternal life, and this life is in His Son.” Given, not earned; eternal life, located in a person. And the last verse of the passage divides the world by that location with the letter's usual plainness: “Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.” Has the Son, has life: the arithmetic admits no third column. What remains is only the letter's own statement of why it was written, and it turns out to have been aimed at this exact certainty all along.

title: Keep Yourselves from Idols
subtitle: 1 John 5:13–21
description: That you may know you have eternal life; prayer for a brother's sin, the three we-knows, and a last line guarding against idols.
paragraphs: The letter now states its own purpose, at the end, the way this writer prefers. “I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life.” Not so that you may hope, or guess, or feel: know. The letter that began with what the witnesses know ends by giving its readers a knowledge of their own, and the knowledge is of a possession, eternal life, held in the present tense by people who believe in the name of the Son of God. Every test in the letter was in service of this sentence. The tests were never meant to leave the readers in suspense about their standing; they were meant to bring them to it.

The confidence has a second address, prayer. “And this is the confidence that we have before Him: If we ask anything according to His will, He hears us.” And the confidence compounds: “And if we know that He hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we already possess what we have asked of Him.” Hearing, in God's case, is having: the asked thing is described as already possessed by the asker who knows he is heard. The letter's assurance runs in both directions at once, toward the life given and toward the ear open, and both are stated as knowledge.

Then the passage takes up a brother's sin one last time, and draws a line the telling carries exactly as drawn. “If anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death, he should ask God, who will give life to those who commit this kind of sin. There is a sin that leads to death; I am not saying he should ask regarding that sin.” Prayer for the sinning brother is the instruction, an act of the same love that opens its hand. But a category stands at the edge of it, a sin that leads to death, and the writer declines to extend the instruction across it. He names no sins for either column, and the telling invents no list for him: “All unrighteousness is sin, yet there is sin that does not lead to death.” The distinction is his; the contents of the lists are left where he left them, unstated.

The letter closes with three sentences that begin we know. “We know that anyone born of God does not keep on sinning; the One who was born of God protects him, and the evil one cannot touch him.” “We know that we are of God, and that the whole world is under the power of the evil one.” The protected and the power are set side by side: the world under the evil one's power, the born-of-God untouchable by him. And the third knowing is the letter's first knowledge come full circle: “And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know Him who is true; and we are in Him who is true” and the sentence finishes on the far side of its own break, “in His Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life.” The Word of life of the first verse is named at the last as the true God and eternal life, and nothing in between has moved him.

Then the letter ends, and it ends the way no reader expects after such heights: “Little children, keep yourselves from idols.” No summary, no farewell, no blessing, just the father's voice one final time and a guard to keep. The telling leaves the line where he leaves it, unexplained. Whatever else the children hold, the knowledge, the confidence, the victory, the testimony, this is the watch he sets at the door as he goes: keep yourselves from idols. With that, the letter of the eyewitness is complete, and the undated group of this series continues with the shortest letters in the New Testament, written to a chosen lady and to a beloved friend.
